name: A. Dessingué
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: A. Dessingué studies how critical thinking and dialogic teaching are taught in Norwegian schools, using teacher interviews and evaluation of professional development programmes in primary and social studies education. The work also examines memory culture after the 2011 terrorist attacks in Norway, looking at memorials, social media and public remembrance through concepts from memory studies and cultural theory. Across both strands, the research connects education, civic engagement and collective responsibility.

name: Allen Clarence Jones
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Allen Clarence Jones studies creative writing games designed to support reading and writing, with a focus on recombinatory writing games that draw on Surrealist and Oulipo techniques. His work combines literary studies and game-design theory with mixed-method action research and surveys to examine creativity, divergent thinking, engagement and play. The studies are set in classroom contexts, including Norwegian high school English, and look at how open versus closed game structures and student involvement as designers affect learning.

name: Brechje Antonet van Osch
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Brechje Antonet van Osch studies bilingual and multilingual language knowledge and processing, including how the term "heritage" is defined and applied in bilingualism research and how earlier-learned languages influence later-learned ones. Her work uses critical literature review, which leads to proposed reporting standards, as well as experiments combining self-paced reading and acceptability judgment tasks with learners of Norwegian from several language backgrounds. The research bears on terminology, research methods and theories of grammatical representation in multilingual speakers.

name: Charlotte Alexandra Wrigley
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Charlotte Alexandra Wrigley is a human geographer who studies how people, animals, technologies and physical environments are entangled, drawing on theories of biopolitics, materiality and multispecies relations. Her work uses empirical fieldwork and analysis of documents such as aviation safety reports to examine bird strike management, conservation of barnacle geese in a former munitions landscape, and the underground in the Russian Arctic, including the Kola Superdeep Borehole and thawing permafrost. Across these studies she looks at how scientific, military, Indigenous and artistic ways of knowing shape airspace, land and subsurface worlds.

name: D. A. Wagner
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: D. A. Wagner studies critical thinking, dialogic teaching and history education in Norwegian schools and teacher education. The work uses interviews, classroom case studies, student assignments and questionnaire surveys with factor analysis and cognitive interviewing to examine teachers' practices, students' discussions of difficult history, historical empathy, and epistemic beliefs about history.

name: Daniel Joe Bowman
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Daniel Joe Bowman studies early twentieth-century American literature and culture, focusing on the relationship between automobiles, horses and national identity. His work uses close literary reading alongside period sources such as automotive periodicals and wartime memoirs, drawing on animal studies and ecological approaches. It covers Osage author John Joseph Mathews's novel Sundown and the First World War American ambulance corps, examining colonialism, Indigenous representation, masculinity and mechanization.

name: David Albert Natvig
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: David Albert Natvig studies bilingualism, heritage languages and language attrition, combining formal theories of morphology and the syntax–phonology interface with sociolinguistic analysis. His work models plural and tense allomorphy in Pennsylvania Dutch and North American Norwegian using frameworks such as Nanosyntax and EFP phonology, and examines how community structure shaped the shift from Norwegian to English in Ulen, Minnesota using census data, local history and interviews. He has also co-authored an introductory text on language attrition covering its linguistic, social and cognitive aspects.

name: David-Alexandre Thomas Wagner
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: David-Alexandre Thomas Wagner studies dialogic teaching in school social studies and history education in Norway, with a focus on teacher professional development. His work examines a one-year development program through students' and teachers' accounts of changes in classroom practice, such as shifts from teacher-centered to student-centered approaches. The application areas are teacher education, critical historical consciousness and civic engagement.

name: Dina Lialikhova
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Dolly Jørgensen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Dolly Jørgensen works in environmental history and the environmental humanities, with a focus on extinction, museums and cultural heritage. Her work uses historical and interpretive analysis of museum displays, conservation practices, emotions and science fiction texts to examine how extinct species, fossil-fuel industrialisation and curated narratives are presented and understood. It also covers topics such as deextinction, urban sanitation and digital ecologies, with relevance to museum practice and heritage interpretation.

name: Eric Dean Rasmussen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Eva Stina Maria Jakobsson
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Finn Arne Jørgensen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Finn Arne Jørgensen studies the relationship between digital technologies and the environment, drawing on environmental humanities and history. His publications examine how surveillance tools such as cameras and sensors shape public relations with wild animals, and how digital public histories frame and contest narratives about places. He also contributes to work on marine litter, using a comparison with beverage container take-back schemes and a business ecosystems approach to explore policy and industry requirements for recycling fishing gear.

name: Geir Bergstrøm
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Geir Skeie
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Geir Skeie studies religious education and the study of religion and worldviews in schools, focusing on Norway. His work combines curriculum and policy analysis, conceptual and philosophical discussion, interviews with teachers and preservice teachers, classroom observation and collaborative action research. Application areas include deep learning reforms, existential questions in teaching, bias-based bullying and inclusive classrooms, teacher practice development, and global education policy on religion.

name: Gitte Westergaard
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Gitte Westergaard studies how cultural objects in museum collections can carry evidence of species extinction and biodiversity loss. Her work treats Hawaiian feather capes ('ahu'ula), made from the plumage of endemic forest birds that are now extinct or threatened, as biocultural artefacts, using them to examine human links to lost species. It points to ways ethnographic collections, and not only natural history museums, can be used to tell extinction stories.

name: Hadle Oftedal Andersen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Hadle Oftedal Andersen studies Norwegian literature of the 1960s, focusing on how writers linked to the journal Profil, including Dag Solstad, Einar Økland and Jan Erik Vold, used humour in their texts. Using close textual analysis and comparison with the traditions they targeted, such as moralistic and national-romantic writing and elevated poetic language, the work shows how humour served to challenge rival poetic practices. The research sits in literary studies and the study of the literary field, with attention to international influences.

name: Ingrid Løland
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Ingrid Løland studies how mountain landscapes can support transformative learning through the lens of biocultural diversity and human-nature connectivity. Her work uses a Kurdish case study and interdisciplinary, narrative-based analysis of mountains as both material and metaphorical places. It looks at how place-based and indigenous knowledge can inform education responses to the Anthropocene and to threats such as ecocide and epistemicide.

name: Janne Stigen Drangsholt
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Janne Stigen Drangsholt works in cultural and media studies, with a focus on television analysis. Her listed publication examines the series The White Lotus through the concepts of utopia and heterotopia, reading the resort island setting as a space that stands apart from ordinary social life. The work applies critical and literary theory to contemporary screen fiction.

name: Jon Skarpeid
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Jonas Fossli Gjersø
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Jonas Fossli Gjersø studies the political economy of global shipping and energy, using historical and geopolitical analysis. His work covers how the pandemic, wars, sanctions, chokepoints and decarbonization efforts have affected shipping markets and freight rates, as well as the history of petroleum governance and knowledge transfer between Norway and China, including the roles of national oil companies. He has also published a review related to the history of imperialism in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

name: Ketil Knutsen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Kjetil Vikhamar Thengs
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Marianne Hafnor Bøe
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Marianne Hafnor Bøe is listed with two publications, from 2022 and 2023, but both carry only the title "Norway" and come with no abstracts or other content. The records give no information about her research areas, methods or application domains, so no specific expertise can be described. A fuller overview would need more detailed publication records.

name: Marie-Theres Fojuth
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Marie-Theres Fojuth studies the cultural history of nature, tourism and museums, with a focus on Norway and the Alpine region. Her work uses historical analysis of travel guides, automobile club materials and landscape narratives to examine how car tourism shaped German images of Norway from the 1920s to the 1960s, including during wartime occupation. She also examines how museums exhibit mountains, time and vulnerable ecosystems in an era of rapid species loss.

name: Markus Eldegard Mindrebø
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Markus Eldegard Mindrebø studies political culture and social relationships in medieval Scandinavia, focusing on the Old Norse-Icelandic kings' sagas and the part played by aristocratic and royal women. He applies network theory and qualitative network analysis to bonds of kinship, friendship and lordship, and has also explored using strategy-game simulation with non-player character modelling to test hypotheses about historical networks.

name: Matthew Robert Holmes
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Matthew Robert Holmes is a historian of science, technology and the environment who studies the relationships between humans, animals and technology, especially introduced species such as the house sparrow in the United States and the mongoose in colonial Jamaica. His archival and case-study work also covers colonial entomology and plantation agriculture, J. B. S. Haldane's ideas on synthetic food, and the public and corporate narratives around genetically modified crops in Britain. He also has a publication on hybrid teaching of the history of Mendelian genetics.

name: Melina Antonia Buns
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Melina Antonia Buns studies the history of environmental politics and policy in the Nordic region, covering institutionalised Nordic cooperation, environmental diplomacy and the making of international environmental law since the 1960s. Her historical research also looks at civil society and consumer activism, including campaigns on disposable packaging and nuclear fuel reprocessing, and at how Nordic countries built a green regional image. Her work draws on case studies of conventions, conferences and social movements, with links to European integration and transboundary pollution.

name: Merja Riitta Stenroos
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Merja Riitta Stenroos studies the history of English, focusing on geographical variation in Old and Middle English and on medieval spelling practices. Her work draws on historical corpora such as the Corpus of Middle English Local Documents and on close study of manuscripts, including those copied by the Tremulous Hand of Worcester. It examines how early writing can be localised and how scribal spelling systems worked, questioning assumptions about dialect reconstruction and spelling-sound correspondence.

name: Nadine Kolb
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Nadine Kolb studies second and third language learning and bilingualism, with attention to how learners' language backgrounds shape their learning and processing. Her work includes a survey-based study of attitudes and self-concept among fifth-grade English learners in Germany, a self-paced reading experiment on grammatical gender and word order in Spanish-speaking learners of German, and methodological and conceptual work on heritage languages and on the use of monolingual comparison groups in bilingualism research. Application areas include early English education, classroom diversity, and research practice in psycholinguistics.

name: Peter Paul Ferry
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Peter Paul Ferry studies nineteenth-century American literature, with a focus on Herman Melville's early sea narratives. Using close textual reading, his work examines how beards function as symbols of otherness, male bonding, and shifting power relations in books such as Typee, Omoo, Mardi and White-Jacket. The research addresses how masculinity is performed and shaped by hierarchy and authority in maritime settings.

name: Roald Berg
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Shayan Aqdas
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Shayan Aqdas studies English language teaching and reading comprehension among Pakistani learners, drawing on schema theory to examine how prior knowledge shapes understanding of new texts. Using a comparison of experimental and control groups of 60 students, comprehension tests and a Likert-scale perception survey, the work tests whether familiar cultural cues in teaching materials improve vocabulary, evaluation and inferential skills. The findings relate to classroom practice and the design of contextualized learning materials for English language learners.

name: Ståle Gundersen
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Ståle Gundersen works in philosophy of mind and philosophy of science, focusing on consciousness, the mind-brain problem and the structure of explanation in psychoanalysis. His work uses conceptual and historical analysis, drawing on current theories of scientific models and mechanistic explanation, to examine Freud's theoretical commitments and how psychoanalysis could be integrated with psychology and neuroscience. He also analyses philosophy of religion arguments, assessing whether the existence of consciousness supports theism.

name: Suzanne Sophie Ros
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Suzanne Sophie Ros works in cultural history, as shown by an afterword that reviews developments in the field and considers where it might head next. The publication is reflective and historiographical in approach, taking stock of past scholarship and directions for future work. Only this one publication is available, so the details of her wider research areas and methods cannot be determined.

name: Torill Irene Hestetræet
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages

name: Tyson Ashley Retz
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Tyson Ashley Retz works on the theory and history of history, and on history education, with a focus on how concepts such as progress are formed, used and contested. His publications use conceptual analysis and comparison of methodological traditions, drawing on R.G. Collingwood, Koselleck and Cambridge school contextualism, to examine historical knowledge, questions and evidence. He applies this to progressive education, the teaching of history in the Anthropocene, and the ethical and political stakes of how the past is represented.

name: Vidar Fagerheim Kalsås
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Vidar Fagerheim Kalsås studies how the Holocaust is taught in Norwegian schools, using interviews with history and social science teachers about their lesson planning and classroom practice. His work looks at the part emotions play in history teaching and at how teachers combine moral lessons from the past with historical thinking and source-based work. The research is grounded in a sociocultural view of history education.

name: Yvonne Wilhelmina Henriette van Baal
department: Department of Cultural Studies and Languages
summary: Yvonne Wilhelmina Henriette van Baal studies the syntax and morphology of Norwegian noun phrases, focusing on grammatical gender, definiteness and determiners. Her work uses elicited production experiments, acceptability judgments and corpus data to examine dialect variation and language change in Norway, and to compare homeland Norwegian with heritage Norwegian spoken in North America. The research tests formal syntactic analyses against these data, including how heritage grammars differ from both the baseline variety and the dominant language, English.

name: Anita Berge
summary: Anita Berge studies how teacher educators in initial teacher education programmes approach teaching for diversity and social justice. Her work develops and applies a transdisciplinary framework that combines epistemic cognition with theories of reflexivity, and uses it to examine the knowledge claims behind the pedagogical decisions of teacher educators in Australia and New Zealand. The focus is on how critical thinking and evaluative views of knowledge shape teacher preparation for diverse classrooms.

name: Aud Torill Meland
summary: Aud Torill Meland studies early childhood education and care in Norway, with a focus on how staff gender shapes children's outdoor physical activity and play in kindergartens. Her work combines accelerometer measurements and systematic observation with document analysis of kindergarten annual plans and discourse analysis of recorded practicum conversations. The application areas are kindergarten practice, curriculum interpretation, and the learning of early childhood student teachers during placements.

name: Barbara Maria Sageidet
summary: Barbara Maria Sageidet studies how young children and their teachers learn about sustainability and the environment through gardens, urban green spaces and local environmental issues such as air quality, mainly in Stavanger, Norway. Her work uses qualitative methods including observations, interviews, surveys, drawings and reflexive thematic analysis, sometimes combined with mapping and quantitative analysis. She also contributes to interdisciplinary case studies and edited volumes on the smart sustainable city, covering policy implementation, organizational change and cross-disciplinary collaboration.

name: Bente Gurine Kvitvær Nordmo
summary: Bente Gurine Kvitvær Nordmo studies how the gender of kindergarten staff relates to the physical activity of 3–5-year-old girls and boys in Norwegian outdoor playgrounds. Her work combines accelerometer measurements, systematic observation and semi-structured staff interviews in case studies of a single kindergarten. The findings cover differences in the types of play staff encourage, children's activity levels, and staff attitudes toward gender and the promotion of activity.

name: Carl Cato Wadel
summary: Carl Cato Wadel studies professional learning and development in early childhood education and care, with a focus on Norwegian kindergartens as learning organizations. His work uses qualitative interviews with kindergarten managers to examine how they understand organizational learning and what they see as marks of a learning kindergarten. The findings highlight joint reflection as central and show that it is hard to build into everyday practice.

name: Elin Kirsti Lie Reikerås
summary: Elin Kirsti Lie Reikerås studies early childhood education and care in Norway and the Nordic countries, covering classroom quality, early cognitive and language development, and children's later academic outcomes. Her work combines longitudinal statistical modelling, such as structural equation modelling, with qualitative case studies, video observation, document analysis, interviews and literature reviews. Further application areas include play with coding toys and computational thinking in early mathematics, special education for children with language difficulties, evaluation policy, and partnerships between universities and kindergartens.

name: Eva Marianne Johansson
summary: Eva Marianne Johansson studies belonging, inclusion and exclusion among children in preschool and early education settings, drawing on the politics of belonging framework. Her work combines video observation case studies, child interviews, and large surveys of educators and parents across several European countries, and also synthesises findings from an international project into policy and practice recommendations. She also researches how teacher educators in Australia and New Zealand use epistemic cognition and reflexivity to teach for diversity and social justice, using surveys and group workshops.

name: Francesca Granone
summary: Francesca Granone studies how young children aged 0–12 learn computational thinking, mathematics and problem-solving through play with coding toys, robots and unplugged materials in early childhood and primary education. Her work uses qualitative case studies, video observation, participatory and inclusive co-design workshops, and systematic and scoping literature reviews, often examining how teachers mediate children's learning. She also addresses inclusion and disability, including neurodiversity, co-research with an autistic researcher, and mediated learning in families of children with Down syndrome.

name: Gunnar Magnus Eidsvåg
summary: Gunnar Magnus Eidsvåg studies early childhood education and care (ECEC), covering children's transition from home into ECEC, how ECEC quality is evaluated in the Nordic countries, and the ethics of care in staff practice. His methods include systematic scoping review, documentary analysis and qualitative interviews with educators, academics and policy makers. The work relates to ECEC policy, institutional practice and professional ethics in Nordic and wider European settings.

name: Johana Evelyn Montalvan Castilla
summary: Johana Evelyn Montalvan Castilla studies how young children learn and take part in urban environments in Stavanger, Norway, covering urban green spaces, outdoor learning, solar energy and STEM education in kindergartens, and children's participation in smart city planning. Her work combines qualitative methods such as observations, interviews and case studies with surveys, statistical analysis and spatial mapping. The findings inform early childhood education practice, sustainability learning, and urban planning and policy for green spaces and child-inclusive cities.

name: Kirsten Halle
summary: Kirsten Halle researches music education in early childhood settings, focusing on singing and musicality among kindergarten teachers and student teachers. Her work applies Cultural-historical Activity Theory to compare studies on musical self-concept and to develop the idea of adult companionship and collective music-making. It has implications for how music is taught in kindergarten teacher education programmes.

name: Kristin Grøsvik
summary: Kristin Grøsvik studies how early childhood education and care teachers in Norway facilitate children's play with coding toys. Using qualitative methods such as video observation, workshops, and semi-structured interviews with video-stimulated recall, and drawing on sociocultural and sustained shared thinking theories, the work examines teachers' self-perceived roles and the pedagogical strategies they use to support children's problem-solving. The research is set in kindergarten settings and relates to early STEM learning and digital play.

name: Lars Yngve Rosell
summary: Lars Yngve Rosell conducts systematic and scoping reviews of research on early childhood education and care (ECEC), with a focus on the Nordic countries. The publications cover how children under three move from home into ECEC and how Nordic ECEC settings were affected by COVID-19, drawing on searches of national and international databases. The work maps study designs, identifies research gaps, and draws out implications for children's adaptation, parent and educator experiences, and resilience in ECEC during crises.

name: Marianne Ree
summary: Marianne Ree studies early childhood education and care (ECEC) for children under three, focusing on how young children take part in the community and how they move from home into ECEC settings. Her work includes a qualitative hermeneutic analysis of interviews with ECEC teachers, informed by Habermas and Yuval-Davis, and a systematic scoping review of research published from 2013 to 2024. The findings relate to teaching practice, institutional frameworks and gaps in research on the youngest children in ECEC.

name: Marianne Undheim
summary: Marianne Undheim studies how digital technology is used and taught in early childhood education and care, with a focus on early childhood teacher education in Norway. Her work combines literature reviews, surveys of teacher educators, curriculum and legal document analysis, and qualitative case studies of young children making animated stories, using frameworks such as social semiotics and multimodality. She also examines educators' beliefs and attitudes about technology and children's right to participate in a Brazil–Norway comparison.

name: Mariella Annika Asikanius
summary: Mariella Annika Asikanius studies how children under three make the transition from home into early childhood education and care (ECEC). Her work uses a systematic scoping review of peer-reviewed studies across national and international databases in several languages, mapping study designs, countries, informants and the concepts examined, such as children's adaptive behavior, stress, structural quality and parents' experiences. The work is relevant to early years education practice and to identifying research gaps for future studies.

name: Monika Kamola
summary: Monika Kamola studies early childhood education and care in Norway, focusing on how teachers support children's play and learning with digital technology such as coding toys. Her work uses qualitative methods including video observation, interviews with video-stimulated recall, workshops and action inquiry, drawing on sociocultural and sustained shared thinking theories. She has also examined young children's sensory experiences, specifically smell, in a kindergarten through collaboration between researchers and practitioners.

name: Ove Bergersen
summary: Ove Bergersen studies early childhood education, focusing on how young children and their teachers learn through gardens, soil and place-based activities. The work uses qualitative methods such as reflexive thematic analysis, participatory and inquiry-based approaches, and analysis of teachers' accounts, and draws on philosophical and educational theory. Application areas include regenerative garden design, education for sustainability and the Anthropocene, and relationships between children and teachers in kindergartens.

name: Sara Esmaeeli
summary: Sara Esmaeeli studies early childhood education and care, focusing on how teacher education prepares future early childhood teachers to use digital technology with children, and on young children's transitions and early literacy. Her work uses systematic and scoping literature reviews alongside survey-based and statistical modelling studies, including surveys of Norwegian teacher educators and a large sample of Norwegian six-year-olds and their parents. The findings apply to teacher education curricula, early childhood practice, and family and preschool support for children's early learning.

name: Stine Elisabeth Vik
summary: Stine Elisabeth Vik studies user-controlled personal assistance for children and young people with disabilities in Norway, using qualitative methods. Her work examines how the independent living ideology works in family settings, where a parent must both care for the child and manage the assistance arrangement. It points to a need to adapt the ideological framework to childhood, treating assistance as a means of building toward future independence.

name: Synne Kristin Nese Skarsaune
summary: Synne Kristin Nese Skarsaune studies how people with profound intellectual and multiple disabilities, who communicate without symbolic language, can be included in qualitative research and professional care. Her work draws on embodied phenomenology, particularly Merleau-Ponty, film analysis, ethnographic fieldwork and conceptual-historical analysis to develop methodological guidance and to rethink empathy as an embodied, always partial process. The application areas are early childhood disability research and professional work with people with profound disabilities.

name: Tove Erna Belland
summary: Tove Erna Belland studies how children under three make the transition from home into early childhood education and care (ECEC). Her work uses a systematic scoping review, searching national and international databases in several languages to map the research on this transition. It covers topics such as children's adaptive behavior, stress, structural quality in ECEC, and the roles and experiences of parents, and it identifies gaps for future research.

name: Tuula Helka Sarvas Skarstein
summary: Tuula Helka Sarvas Skarstein studies early childhood education in Norway, focusing on science learning for toddlers in natural environments and on children's critical thinking. Her work uses qualitative interviews with early childhood teachers and educators, analysed thematically, to understand their views and practices. The findings relate to kindergarten and ECEC settings, outdoor play and learning, and the support needed for educators.

name: Wilfried Klaas Smidt
summary: Wilfried Klaas Smidt studies leadership in early childhood education and care, focusing on how German preschool leaders' behaviors group into distinct styles. His work uses staff ratings of leaders and person-centered statistical methods, including two-level latent profile analysis and multinomial logistic regression, to link these styles to leaders' childcare qualifications and preschool size. The findings are relevant to leadership training and policy in early childhood education.

name: Yngve Rosell
summary: Yngve Rosell studies how the youngest children, aged 1 to 3, take part in community life in early childhood education and care settings. The work uses qualitative, hermeneutic analysis of semi-structured interviews with ECEC teachers, drawing on Habermas's lifeworld and system concepts and Yuval-Davis's theory of belonging. It examines how teachers handle institutional frames and children's own experiences and expressions when creating opportunities for community.

name: Agnes Wigestrand Hoftun
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Agnes Wigestrand Hoftun studies how writers use digital language resources when correcting errors in their first language, focusing on Norwegian Nynorsk. Her work uses think-aloud methods with screen and audio recordings of master's students, analysed with an annotation protocol for consultation behavior. The findings bear on dictionary design and on teaching norm and metalinguistic knowledge in Norwegian language education.

name: Alessandro Falcetta
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Alessandro Falcetta studies the parable of the Good Samaritan in Luke's Gospel, reading it through modern philosophical frameworks. His work applies Axel Honneth's theory of recognition and Alfred North Whitehead's process philosophy to explain interpretive problems in the text and to clarify what 'neighbour' means. The readings link biblical interpretation with ethical questions about unconditional recognition, crossing social boundaries and ecological relationships.

name: Anastasia Hanukaev
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Anastasia Hanukaev studies intercultural learning in English as a foreign language classrooms in Norwegian lower secondary schools. Her case studies use teacher interviews and learner focus groups to examine how an e-portfolio of intercultural competence supports reflection and flexible learning spaces, and how classroom tasks help pupils take the perspectives of others. The work leads to pedagogical recommendations for language teachers on developing intercultural competence.

name: Anders Otterbech Jølbo Myrset
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Anders Otterbech Jølbo Myrset studies second language pragmatics with young learners of English, focusing on speech acts such as requests, politeness, and learners' metapragmatic awareness in primary school EFL classrooms, mainly in Norway. His work uses group interviews, thematic analysis, video-prompted discourse completion tests and appraisal tasks, and also tests concept-based instruction grounded in sociocultural theory. It extends to teacher education, classroom activities and learner feedback on pragmatics teaching, and includes edited and authored books on the topic.

name: Andreas Åvitsland
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Andreas Åvitsland studies physical activity, active travel and health among Norwegian adolescents, using data from the School In Motion project. His work applies questionnaires, fitness tests, GIS-based measures of the built environment, decision tree analysis and linear mixed-effect models. Topics include how demographic and environmental factors shape walking, cycling or motorized travel to school, and how cardiorespiratory and muscular fitness relate to health-related quality of life.

name: Ann Elisabeth Laksfoss Cardozo
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Ann Elisabeth Laksfoss Cardozo studies international retirement migration, focusing on Norwegian seniors who spend time or settle in Alicante, Spain. Her work examines how elderly care and healthcare services have been offshored beyond the nation-state, including the rise and closure of publicly funded Norwegian care centres abroad. It also considers how European mobility, economic factors and the COVID-19 pandemic shaped these arrangements.

name: Arne Jakobsen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Arne Jakobsen studies mathematics education, with a focus on how primary mathematics is taught, how teachers' knowledge is measured, and how teachers develop professionally. The work uses systematic literature review, qualitative case studies, lesson study, classroom observation frameworks and statistical comparison of teacher-knowledge test data. Application settings include Malawi, South Africa, Norway and Slovakia, covering multilingual classrooms, teaching resources, mathematical modelling and cross-national assessment of teacher knowledge.

name: Berit Aarrestad
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Berit Aarrestad studies applied drama as an educational approach, focusing on how performance-based learning affects students' critical thinking, cultural identity and political awareness. Her work uses Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis to explore the experiences of Palestinian exchange students taking a drama and intercultural communication course in Norway. It addresses higher education settings, educational reform and the use of drama for self-expression and social activism.

name: Cathrine Holmen Hagum
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Cathrine Holmen Hagum studies the training load, wellbeing and injury risk of Norwegian student athletes who combine high school with elite sport. Her work uses cross-sectional questionnaires, including the Relational Coordination Survey and a training distress scale, as well as a randomised controlled trial of individualised, progressive training in football and handball players. It looks at communication among athletes, coaches, teachers, parents and health personnel, and at how training volume and distress differ by gender, sport and school year.

name: Cecilie Aarøe
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Cecilie Aarøe studies the experiences of German refugees who came to Denmark at the end of World War II, focusing on one family who fled in March 1945 and were later held in Danish refugee camps. She uses a microhistory approach called singularisation, building a narrative from the family's oral and written testimonies rather than using their story as an example of wider social structures. Her work also contributes to methodological debates in microhistory and to research on post-war refugee history.

name: Cecilie Waallann Brown
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Cecilie Waallann Brown researches critical visual literacy and critical literacy in English as a foreign language education, with attention to intercultural learning and symbolic competence. Her work includes classroom case studies with Norwegian upper secondary learners, using thematic analysis of learner redesigns, written reflections and focus group dialogue about images, alongside theoretical work drawing on critical literacy models. More recently she has examined how pre-service English teachers engage critically with multimodal texts.

name: Dag Ove Granås Hovdal
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Dag Ove Granås Hovdal studies physical education in Norwegian secondary schools, focusing on how student effort is understood, taught and assessed. His qualitative work, grounded in pragmatist educational philosophy, combines classroom observation, 360-degree video recordings and stimulated recall interviews with teachers and students. The research addresses teacher assessment practices and how they shape students' individual and social actions in lessons.

name: Eli Flatekval
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Eli Flatekval studies how teacher educators in Norway can build interdisciplinary professional communities for teaching about sustainable development. The research uses an exploratory, participatory qualitative design, analysing audio recordings of interdisciplinary workshops with teacher educators and drawing on transformative learning and dialogue theory. It focuses on how dialogue around concepts such as action competence and systems thinking shapes collaboration in teacher education.

name: Eva Leibinger
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Eva Leibinger studies how physical fitness relates to health-related quality of life in young people. Her work uses a cross-sectional design with nearly 2,000 Norwegian 14-year-olds, combining field-based tests of running endurance and muscular strength with the KIDSCREEN-27 questionnaire, analysed through linear mixed-effects models. The findings are relevant to adolescent health, school-based physical activity and public health.

name: Hanne Egenæs Staurseth
department: Department of Education and Sports Science

name: Hans Erik Bugge
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Hans Erik Bugge's publications span archetypal psychology and education research. One chapter applies archetypal psychology to Norway's collective meaning-making after the 22 July attacks, looking at rose parades and a children's song as examples of memorialisation. A separate case study uses interviews, observation and a survey to examine how primary school teachers see their role and manage classrooms where digital technology is heavily used.

name: Hans Geir Aasmundsen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Hans Geir Aasmundsen studies megachurches and Pentecostal Christianity in Latin America, using comparative case studies of congregations in Buenos Aires, Guatemala City, Asunción and Mexico City. The work examines how these churches are organised, including leadership, cell groups, theology, links to wider Pentecostal networks, media use, evangelization and membership. It also considers the factors behind their growth, with relevance to the sociology of religion and religious change in the region.

name: Hein Berdinesen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Hein Berdinesen studies school leadership, inclusive education and teachers' professional development in Norwegian schools. The work uses qualitative methods, including interviews, observations, reflexive thematic analysis and stepwise-deductive inductive analysis. It examines how school leaders and teachers collaborate within policy and organisational frameworks such as municipal inclusion efforts and the full-day school pilot.

name: Håvard Myklebust
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Håvard Myklebust studies the biomechanics of cross-country skiing, using inertial measurement units to capture movement data from well-trained skiers. His work compares uphill V2 skating on asphalt, treadmill and snow, examining hip motion, lateral displacement and pole push timing under controlled speed and incline. The findings relate to how well roller ski training matches on-snow skiing and to possible equipment improvements for Nordic winter sports training.

name: Ingeborg Knævelsrud
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Ingeborg Knævelsrud studies how teacher educators in Norway can build interdisciplinary professional communities for teaching about sustainable development. The work uses an exploratory, participatory qualitative design, analysing audio recordings of interdisciplinary workshops in which the researchers also took part. It draws on transformative learning and dialogue to examine how teacher educators discuss concepts such as action competence, systems thinking and critical thinking.

name: Ingri Dommersnes Jølbo
department: Department of Education and Sports Science

name: Ingrid Hilmer
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Ingrid Hilmer works on literature education and its role in teaching about sustainable development. Her article uses close reading of a Norwegian children's novel, Arne Svingen's En himmel full av skyer, to examine how the concept of wicked problems can frame pupils' encounters with uncertainty, multiple scales of time and place, and demands for responsibility. The work applies this literary analysis to school-based sustainability education.

name: Ingunn Eikeland
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Ingunn Eikeland studies how schools respond to student diversity through differentiation, including differentiated instruction and ability grouping. Her work uses a configurative literature review of 28 international papers to map how the concept is framed, from individualization to adaptation within classrooms. It points to a gap in research at the organizational and policy level and argues for a more system-oriented view of inclusive education.

name: Irina Diaz de Leon
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Irina Diaz de Leon studies eating disorders and disordered eating among athletes, focusing on how well coaches can recognise symptoms. Her work translates and validates a questionnaire into Norwegian and uses factor analysis on survey responses from several hundred coaches to identify symptom groupings and differences in observation by coaching experience. The findings relate to sport mental health and to education and professional development for coaches.

name: James Jacob Thomson
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: James Jacob Thomson studies how upper secondary pupils write essays in English, with a focus on signposting, the explicit marking of relations and structure in a text. His work combines corpus analysis of pupil essays in several genres from Swedish, Norwegian and British schools with teacher interviews to examine both pupil usage and classroom instruction. The findings relate to writing instruction and the teaching of textual organisation in secondary education.

name: Janne Fauskanger
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Janne Fauskanger studies mathematics teaching and teacher education, with a focus on how teaching quality is assessed and how teachers learn through professional development. Her work combines classroom observation instrument validation (Delphi technique, generalizability theory), practice-based approaches such as rehearsals and teacher time outs, lesson study, and video-based case studies of teacher educators' mathematical language. It spans Norwegian primary schools, Malawian primary mathematics and early-years teacher education.

name: Kristine Marie Olsen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Kristine Marie Olsen studies how university teacher educators and primary school staff can work together to develop play-based approaches to teaching school subjects, with a focus on science. Her work describes a collaborative partnership project in which teachers and teacher educators jointly designed and carried out teacher-initiated, subject-specific play, and uses the ideas of third space and community of inquiry to analyse the collaboration. It is relevant to teacher education, school-university partnerships and primary science didactics.

name: Lars Rune Waage
department: Department of Education and Sports Science

name: Magne Ove Rogne
department: Department of Education and Sports Science

name: Marianne Sandvik Tveitnes
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Marianne Sandvik Tveitnes studies inclusive education and special education in Norway, covering teachers' professional knowledge, the mentoring of newly qualified teachers, and teacher education. She also researches educational-psychological services, looking at how counsellors involve children in decisions and how interprofessional collaboration relates to their job satisfaction and intention to leave. Her methods include large-scale surveys with structural equation modelling, focus groups and interviews analysed thematically, and intervention studies using digital problem-based cases.

name: Marie Smith-Solbakken
department: Department of Education and Sports Science

name: Marieke Gerdien Bruin
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Marieke Gerdien Bruin studies inclusion, participation and social justice in education, covering both primary school classrooms and vocational education and training (VET) for young people at risk of social exclusion. Her work relies mainly on qualitative interviews analysed thematically, cross-national comparison across Norway and the Baltic states, critical re-analysis of earlier studies, and co-created intervention studies with VET teachers. It draws on recognition theory, sociocultural theory and social capital, and addresses teacher-student relationships, school dropout, support systems and teacher development.

name: Merete Hagen Helland
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Merete Hagen Helland studies school food and food education in Norwegian primary schools. Her work includes a comparison of free and packed school lunches, using meal photographs, a family affluence questionnaire and statistical tests to relate food quality to socioeconomic background. She also uses qualitative interviews with teachers and school leaders to examine how the Food and Health subject is taught in grades 1-4, including the resources and teaching aids used.

name: Mette Irene Hvalby
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Mette Irene Hvalby studies mentoring and professional development in Norwegian teacher education and early career teaching. Using focus groups, surveys and interviews analysed thematically and descriptively, her work looks at how mentors guide novice teachers through induction programmes, including inclusive education and teacher well-being. She also examines how suitability assessments of students in professional programmes are carried out and how mentors experience them, including during and after the COVID-19 pandemic.

name: Milica Savic
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Milica Savic studies second language pragmatics with young learners of English, focusing on politeness, speech acts, requests and metapragmatic awareness in primary and lower secondary EFL classrooms in Norway, Cyprus and elsewhere in Europe. Her work uses thematic analysis of group interviews and task-based discussions, along with participant-centred data collection methods suited to children, and she has authored and co-edited books on young learner pragmatics and its teaching. She also examines English teacher education and classroom practice, including critical visual literacy, multimodal texts and intercultural learning.

name: Milla Saara Anneli Saarinen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Milla Saara Anneli Saarinen studies the psychosocial development of young athletes, including how achievement goals, perceived performance and athletic identity relate to self-esteem among student-athletes in Norwegian lower secondary sport schools, using survey data and regression-based conditional process analysis. She also works on higher education teaching in sport and exercise science, examining how technology-enhanced learning and artificial intelligence can be designed to include dual-career athletes, international students and neurodivergent learners. Her work links motivation theory and pedagogical frameworks to practice in youth sport and university education.

name: Nils Olav Østrem
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Nils Olav Østrem studies how emotions were expressed in the letters of early Norwegian immigrants to America, drawing on correspondence from 1838 to 1848 sent to family, neighbours and friends. The work analyses the balance of positive and negative feelings in these letters and how emotional appeals may have encouraged further emigration from Norway. It sits within migration history and the history of emotions.

name: Nina Helgevold
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Nina Helgevold studies teacher education and teacher professional development, with a strong focus on lesson study in Norwegian, Malawian and online or hybrid settings. Her work uses case studies, interviews, surveys, focus groups and qualitative content analysis to examine what sustains school-based learning, how student teachers connect theory and practice through digital problem-based cases, and how university and school partnerships build shared knowledge. She also looks at classroom management in technology-rich primary classrooms and at play-based science teaching in primary school.

name: Nina Lazarevic
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Nina Lazarevic studies English language teacher education, focusing on how future and practising teachers develop intercultural communicative competence, grammar teaching skills and materials design skills. Her work uses qualitative methods such as semi-structured interviews, thematic analysis and content analysis of teacher assignments. The contexts include internationalised university campuses in the United States and Norway, a year-long professional development course for in-service teachers, and a materials design course for pre-service teachers.

name: Pauline Book
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Pauline Book studies how teacher educators can work across disciplines to teach sustainability, focusing on Education for Sustainable Development in Norwegian teacher education. Her work uses an exploratory, participatory qualitative design, analysing audio recordings of interdisciplinary workshops in which she also took part. It examines how dialogue and critical reflection among teacher educators shape shared understandings of concepts such as systems thinking and action competence.

name: Radel James Eumague Gacumo
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Radel James Eumague Gacumo studies early childhood literacy, focusing on how gender, equity, diversity and inclusion are shaped through picturebooks, digital texts and wordless animated films. The work draws on multimodal and sensory literacy frameworks together with queer theory, childhood studies and postcolonial perspectives, using conceptual analysis, case studies of kindergarten shared reading and close analysis of film. He also uses queer collaborative autoethnography to examine the experiences of queer Asian diasporic researchers.

name: Raymond Bjuland
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Raymond Bjuland studies mathematics teacher education, with a focus on how teachers learn through lesson study. He uses commognitive theory to analyse video recordings of reflection meetings held by Norwegian lower secondary school teachers, examining patterns in their pedagogical discourse about student learning. He has also contributed a memorial tribute to the mathematics education researcher Simon Goodchild.

name: Reidar Mosvold
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Reidar Mosvold studies mathematics teaching and teacher learning, with a focus on teacher questioning, instructional quality and the mathematical knowledge teachers need for teaching. His work uses classroom video, co-planning and lesson study recordings, observation instruments (including Delphi and generalizability methods) and discourse analysis, in Norwegian and Malawian primary and secondary settings. It also looks at how mathematics teacher educators think about teaching, justice and teacher knowledge, and at methods for studying that knowledge.

name: Sebastian Schanche Sandgren
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Sebastian Schanche Sandgren studies eating disorders and muscle dysmorphia in athletes and people who do resistance training, with attention to how symptoms are detected, assessed and supported. His work combines questionnaire development and factor analysis, cross-sectional surveys, interviews and focus groups, a systematic review, and intervention development and feasibility testing. Application areas include sport, coaching, exercise and health professional practice, and early self-help and prevention resources, mainly in Norway.

name: Shaher Ahmmad Ibrahim Shalfawi
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Shaher Ahmmad Ibrahim Shalfawi studies physical activity, training load and physical performance in children, student athletes and elite youth soccer players. His work combines randomised controlled trials, cross-sectional surveys and accelerometer-based observation to examine training interventions, injury prevalence, training distress, and communication among the people around young athletes. Application areas include kindergarten play settings, Norwegian sports academy schools and soccer team training.

name: Silje Eikanger Kvalø
department: Department of Education and Sports Science

name: Silje Henriette Amalia Normand
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Silje Henriette Amalia Normand studies how migrants access and remain in the teaching profession in Norway, focusing on teacher education, recognition of foreign credentials, and language requirements. Her work uses in-depth interviews with institutional actors, migrant teachers, teacher educators and intermediary organisations to examine the gap between policy aims of diversity and the procedures people encounter. It contributes to debates on diversity governance, professional recognition and belonging in higher education and the welfare state.

name: Sindre Mikal Dyrstad
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Sindre Mikal Dyrstad studies physical activity and exercise interventions for health, with a focus on people receiving opioid agonist therapy and on adolescents in school settings. His work combines pilot and randomized controlled trials, systematic review, cross-sectional analysis, observational follow-up and qualitative interviews to examine outcomes such as fitness, psychological distress, quality of life, active travel and programme participation. Applications include outpatient addiction care, school-based physical activity and teacher implementation, and community lifestyle-change services.

name: Sofija Svendsen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Sofija Svendsen studies children's literature, focusing on bilingual Sámi-Norwegian picture books and their use in literature education. Her work applies picturebook research, multilingual picturebook studies and ecocritical fable theory to interpret animal stories that raise questions of identity and belonging. She links this textual analysis to Sámi pedagogy and to teaching Norwegian and Sámi language and literature.

name: Tanu Biswas
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Tanu Biswas works on childism and decolonial theory, examining how adult-centred and Eurocentric assumptions shape education, philosophy and childhood studies. Using conceptual and philosophical analysis, critical readings of textbooks and legal testimonies, collaborative writing and post-qualitative slow research with children, she studies topics such as school strikes for climate, child climate litigants, teacher education in Norway and tools for measuring adultcentric bias. Her work addresses education policy, intergenerational justice, children's participation rights and climate justice.

name: Tarja Irene Tikkanen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Tarja Irene Tikkanen studies vocational education and training (VET) and how it supports at-risk and vulnerable young people in Norway and the Baltic countries, looking at school dropout, inclusion, empowerment and the move from school to work. Her work uses comparative policy analysis, secondary statistical analysis, document studies and qualitative interviews, drawing on socio-ecological, resilience and skill formation frameworks. She has also studied how Norwegian teacher education institutions interpret and put into practice professional digital competence at management level.

name: Thomas Bjørnsen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Thomas Bjørnsen studies exercise physiology and strength and conditioning, using randomized crossover trials, EMG, force plate and motion capture testing, and systematic reviews with meta-analysis. His work covers dietary supplementation and vascular function, trunk muscle activation and core training, blood flow restriction resistance exercise, and force-velocity profiling for jump performance. Participants range from healthy recreational adults to national-level junior and female handball athletes.

name: Vidar Kjetilstad
department: Department of Education and Sports Science

name: Wenche Olivia Sigurdsen
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Wenche Olivia Sigurdsen studies physical education in Norwegian secondary schools, focusing on how teachers assess student effort and how those assessments shape what students do and think. Her work takes a pragmatist, educational perspective and combines classroom observation, 360-degree video recordings and stimulated recall interviews with teachers and students, analysed thematically. The research bears on assessment practice and curriculum implementation in school PE teaching.

name: Åge Vigane
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Åge Vigane studies friluftsliv, the Norwegian tradition of outdoor life, as an approach to teaching in higher education. His work uses qualitative analysis of open-ended student questionnaires from an EU-funded international hiking programme to look at resilience, environmental awareness and intercultural learning. The findings relate to teacher education and outdoor pedagogy across European universities.

name: Åsmund Lillevik Gjære
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Åsmund Lillevik Gjære studies primary mathematics teaching in Norway, focusing on how teachers use challenging tasks within the Developmental Education in Mathematics reform approach. Using case studies based on video-recorded classroom lessons, the work examines how teacher questioning shapes the difficulty of tasks and what dilemmas teachers face when putting reform-oriented methods into practice. The findings are applied to curriculum material design, teacher professional development and the implementation of educational reform.

name: Øystein Nybøe
department: Department of Education and Sports Science
summary: Øystein Nybøe studies inclusive education in primary schools, focusing on how everyday interactions between teachers and students support student participation. His work draws on interviews with teachers and fifth-grade students in Norway, analysed through reflexive thematic analysis and interpreted with Honneth's recognition theory. The findings relate qualities such as care, trust, respect and mutual joy to classroom practices that open space for participation.

name: Ann Kristin Kolstø-Johansen
department: Faculty of Arts and Education (department not stated)
summary: Ann Kristin Kolstø-Johansen studies classroom teaching quality in upper secondary education, focusing on whether a widely used classroom observation instrument works in Norwegian schools. Her work uses video-recorded lessons scored by certified raters and applies two-level statistical models to nested data from academic and vocational classrooms to examine the instrument's structure and reliability. The findings also relate teaching quality dimensions to study track and teacher characteristics.

name: Elisabeth Stray Gausel
department: Faculty of Arts and Education (department not stated)
summary: Elisabeth Stray Gausel studies how smell can be used to enrich children's learning and sensory experiences in museum settings. Her case study in a Norwegian science museum added abstract scents, housed in wooden boxes along an adventure trail, to an exhibition based on 'The Three Little Pigs', and drew on a social theory of learning. The work was carried out through collaboration between academia and industry and ends with reflections and recommendations for future exhibitions that pair odors with storytelling.

name: Hallvor Lyngstad
department: Faculty of Arts and Education (department not stated)

name: Kari-Anne Svensen Malmo
department: Faculty of Arts and Education (department not stated)

name: Andréa Aparecida Goncalves Nes
summary: Andréa Aparecida Goncalves Nes studies nursing education, focusing on digital and simulation-based support for student learning, mentoring and assessment in clinical practice, and on palliative care nursing. Her work combines qualitative interviews and focus groups, scoping reviews, and cross-cultural translation and psychometric validation of instruments measuring student self-efficacy and mentor competence in Norway and Brazil. Application areas include mental health placements, nursing homes, postgraduate palliative care training and digital health services in home-based palliative care.

name: Angelena Ursula Moore
summary: Angelena Ursula Moore studies how working while unwell (presenteeism) affects nurses and the safety of patient care in emergency and primary care settings. Her work uses qualitative methods, drawing on interviews with nurses at out-of-hours primary care facilities in Norway to examine work ethics, workplace stress and coping strategies. The findings relate to occupational health, healthcare quality and patient safety in acute care.

name: Anne Gunn Dovland Vassbø
summary: Anne Gunn Dovland Vassbø works on ethics education for healthcare personnel, with a focus on care ethics and the development of ethical competence and moral sensitivity. Her publication builds a theoretical model through hermeneutic reading of work by caring theorists and applies it to virtual reality learning environments. The application domain is training health professionals in ethical reflection and decision-making through simulated scenarios.

name: Anne Marie Gausel
summary: Anne Marie Gausel studies pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain and low back pain, combining interviews with women, questionnaire cohort data and statistical modelling of pain courses and their links to weight gain, physical activity, disability and quality of life. She also researches how chiropractors in Norway view and use evidence-based practice and maintenance care, using national surveys. Her work applies to women's health, musculoskeletal care and clinical practice in chiropractic.

name: Bente Kristin Høgmo
summary: Bente Kristin Høgmo studies nursing and public health care for families, with a focus on the postnatal period, parenthood and the sexual and reproductive health of refugee youth. Her work uses qualitative methods, including meta-ethnography to synthesize existing studies and phenomenological interviews with mothers and fathers. The findings address how nurses, parents, LGBTQ+ families and young refugees experience maternal and child health services, and what this means for culturally sensitive and inclusive care.

name: Birgitta Haga Gripsrud
summary: Birgitta Haga Gripsrud studies care ethics and the relational side of professional healthcare, focusing on nurses, nursing home staff and physicians in Norway. Her work uses qualitative methods such as focus groups, ethnographic fieldwork and interviews with phenomenological and depth-hermeneutic analysis, along with a scoping review and policy document analysis. Topics include how technology and welfare-state structures affect ideals of care, how care is treated in nursing education, and how staff experience and communicate about death in long-term care. She has also contributed to a protocol for a breast cancer biobank study that combines liquid biopsies with patient-reported outcomes.

name: C. Furskog-Risa
summary: C. Furskog-Risa studies midwifery education and practice, with a focus on simulation-based learning, clinical placement and how midwifery programmes and professional scope differ across Europe and sub-Saharan Africa. The work also examines maternal and reproductive health care, including contraceptive counselling in Tanzania, interprofessional care for vulnerable pregnant women in Norway, and follow-up after gestational diabetes. Methods include qualitative interviews and thematic analysis, questionnaires and descriptive statistics, mixed-methods designs, and systematic reviews or meta-syntheses.

name: Camilla Ann-Louise Koskinen
summary: Camilla Ann-Louise Koskinen conducts caring science research on health, suffering, dignity and life changes, using mainly qualitative methods such as in-depth interviews, thematic analysis, hermeneutic approaches and systematic reviews or meta-ethnography. Her work covers the experiences of men facing life transitions, people with long-term illness, people affected by parental or paternal alienation, and people who have left high-cost religious groups. She also studies nursing and health care education, including students' development as caring nurses, ethical competence, virtual reality for ethics training, and educator competence measured through surveys and statistical modelling.

name: Christina Tølbøl Frøiland
summary: Christina Tølbøl Frøiland studies clinical nursing education and care quality in Norwegian settings, with a focus on mentorship of first-year nursing students in nursing home placements and on assessment discussions between students, mentors and nurse educators. She uses qualitative methods such as interviews, focus groups, observation and co-creative workshops to develop and evaluate digital educational resources for mentors and nurse educators. She has also interviewed healthcare professionals about quality of care and patient safety for older adults in cancer long-term follow-up clinics.

name: Eileen Oftedal
summary: Eileen Oftedal studies emotional dysregulation, alexithymia and personality functioning in patients treated for personality disorders in specialist outpatient mental health services in Norway. Her work uses large multi-site quality registry data, linear mixed models and psychometric methods such as confirmatory factor analysis to track change during treatment and to compare mentalization-based and non-manualized therapies. She has also carried out a qualitative interview study of therapeutic writing within a group programme for binge eating disorder.

name: Ellen Ramvi
summary: Ellen Ramvi studies how healthcare professionals in Norway experience and practise care, with a focus on how digital and other technologies affect relational and ethical aspects of caregiving in general practice and hospital and municipal services. Her work also examines the emotional experiences of nursing home staff, including close relationships with residents who die and how death is, or is not, talked about. She uses qualitative methods such as interviews, focus groups, ethnographic fieldwork, interpretative phenomenological and depth-hermeneutic analysis, and a scoping review, drawing on care ethics and psychoanalytic perspectives.

name: Eva Christina Furskog-Risa
summary: Eva Christina Furskog-Risa studies midwifery and maternal health, with a focus on simulation-based education for nursing and midwifery students in Tanzania and Malawi, particularly for preventing and managing postpartum haemorrhage. Her work combines qualitative methods (interviews, focus groups, thematic and content analysis) with quasi-experimental, cross-sectional and mixed-method designs to assess learning outcomes and educators' and students' experiences. She also examines women's lived experience of pregnancy-related pelvic girdle pain and midwives' views on normal birth across the Nordic and Baltic regions.

name: Gry Ciekals Wallgren
summary: Gry Ciekals Wallgren conducts qualitative caring science research on men's health, covering how men experience life transitions, loss, suffering and meaning, including fathers affected by paternal alienation. She also studies how doctors and nurses in Norwegian hospitals recognise and acknowledge the end of life in patients with cancer, and how organisational structures shape this. Her work relies on in-depth interviews analysed with thematic or content analysis, within hermeneutic and caritative caring theory frameworks, and applies to palliative care, hospital practice and men's wellbeing.

name: Hege Bjøkne Wathne
summary: Hege Bjøkne Wathne studies nurse-assisted eHealth and remote patient monitoring for self-management support after hospital discharge, focusing on patients with heart failure and colorectal cancer. Her work combines qualitative interviews, observation, mixed methods analysis of platform usage data, an integrative literature review and trial protocols to examine acceptability, usability, nurse workload and research recruitment. The studies are set in Norwegian hospitals and aim to inform the design, evaluation and implementation of digital follow-up care.

name: Ida Helene Mykkeltveit
summary: Ida Helene Mykkeltveit studies how simulation can be used in training clinical supervisors of nursing and midwifery students. Her work uses a qualitative design, with focus groups and written reflections analysed thematically, to examine how midwives and specialist nurses experience an interprofessional supervision course. It covers the student-supervisor relationship, communication and learning in clinical placements.

name: Ingela Jobe
summary: Ingela Jobe studies dementia care in nursing homes, focusing on how documented life stories are created and used by assistant nurses in everyday practice. Her work uses qualitative methods, including semi-structured focus group interviews analyzed with content analysis. The research relates to person-centered care and how care staff can personalize support for people living with dementia.

name: Inger Johanne Bergerød
summary: Inger Johanne Bergerød studies resilience, quality and patient safety in health and welfare services, with a focus on elderly care, cancer care and child welfare. Her work uses systematic reviews, qualitative interviews, document analysis, consensus methods and mixed-methods co-design to examine leadership, staff wellbeing, involvement of next of kin and informal caregivers, and regulatory inspection. It is applied to improving care organizations, supporting leaders, and informing supervisory practice in Norway and internationally.

name: Janet Bakken
summary: Janet Bakken studies end-of-life and palliative care, focusing on how patients experience facing death and how doctors and nurses recognise and acknowledge that a patient is dying. Her work uses qualitative methods such as interviews with content analysis and a meta-ethnography synthesising studies, alongside a mixed-methods evaluation of a web-based palliative care pathway. The applications are in hospital cancer care, organisational structures for timely palliative care, and care delivery across services in Norway.

name: Kari Kaldestad
summary: Kari Kaldestad conducts qualitative caring science research, mainly using in-depth and focus-group interviews analysed with hermeneutic and thematic methods. Her work examines health, suffering, meaning, dignity and ethical values in men going through life transitions and paternal alienation, in nurses caring for people with substance use disorder, and in frail older women receiving municipal care. She also works on multi-professional ethical competence in healthcare and on supervisor education grounded in caring science.

name: Kine Gjesdal
summary: Kine Gjesdal studies chronic pain management in primary care, including the design and testing of personalized, multidisciplinary group-based interventions delivered through municipal health services. Her work uses co-development, feasibility and longitudinal cohort designs with questionnaire outcomes such as health literacy, quality of life, sleep and medication use. She also contributes to national registry-linkage research in Norway describing people with chronic pain and long-term opioid users, covering diagnoses, prescribing and socioeconomic factors.

name: Kjetil Moen
summary: Kjetil Moen's work in this publication focuses on the existential experiences of patients with life-threatening illness who are facing death, within palliative and end-of-life care. It uses a meta-ethnography, a method for systematically synthesising qualitative interview studies, to combine findings from 317 patients across published research. The results describe how patients seek meaning, hope, connection and belonging, and the authors draw implications for clinical practice and education in end-of-life care.

name: Kristina Sundt Eriksen
summary: Kristina Sundt Eriksen studies recovery after colorectal cancer surgery in people aged 80 and older. Her work combines in-depth interviews analysed with content analysis and a cross-sectional survey of survivors, looking at coping, sense of coherence, social support and health problems. The findings relate to nursing and follow-up care, especially discharge and support for older patients.

name: Kristine Rørtveit
summary: Kristine Rørtveit conducts qualitative health research in palliative care and mental health services. Her work uses meta-ethnography, narrative synthesis, interviews and theory-driven analysis to study how patients experience facing death, suicidal crisis and eating disorder treatment. She also examines how frontline leaders put clinical guidelines into practice in Norwegian psychiatric care, and how safe, resilient care can be supported.

name: Linda Nyholm
summary: Linda Nyholm studies how social and humanoid robots can be designed and used in health and care settings, with a focus on medication counselling in community pharmacies and exercise programs for older people living at home. Her work relies mainly on qualitative methods such as interviews, focus groups, thematic analysis, co-design, role-play and hierarchical task analysis, and also includes a scoping review of voice use in nursing. Other publications address nursing and caring topics, including intensive care nurses' views on donation after circulatory death and experiences of care after leaving a religious community.

name: Linda Susanne Estman
summary: Linda Susanne Estman conducts qualitative and theoretical research in caring science, focusing on nursing ethics, caring theory and the human side of health technology. Her studies use interviews with nurses, home care workers, young adults and people who left religious communities, analysed with reflexive thematic analysis, content analysis and critical incident technique, and she also develops hermeneutic methods and quality frameworks for interpretive research. Application areas include social robots, virtual reality ethics training and language-model medication counselling, as well as organ donation, telehomecare sustainability and occupational health.

name: Line Johanne Øvrebø
summary: Line Johanne Øvrebø studies how the clinical competence of postgraduate critical care nursing students is assessed during practice placements, with a focus on Norway. Her work combines qualitative methods, including focus group and individual interviews with students, preceptors and teachers, with document analysis and an integrative literature review. The findings apply to nursing education, placement supervision and the design of assessment criteria and tools shared by universities and clinical practice.
